ai-at-work.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo
ai-at-work.excerpt: A memo circulated earlier this year reportedly claimed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited a female technology executive to spy on Nvidia's CEO.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A Chinese intelligence officer allegedly recruited a tech executive to gather intelligence on Nvidia's CEO, according to a US intelligence memo making the rounds this year. This matters to digital workplace pros because it's a stark reminder that corporate espionage targeting tech leadership is real and often happens through social engineering and personal relationships rather than dramatic movie heists. If you're building internal security programs and thinking "that could never happen here," you're probably the person it will happen to first.

ai-at-work.title: Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push
ai-at-work.excerpt: Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks. The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the s
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Thinking Machines just dropped Inkling 2 Small, a new language model designed to automate AI training work, while simultaneously hunting for $5 billion in fresh funding. For workplace tech leaders, this matters because automation of AI training could eventually streamline how your organization builds and deploys custom AI tools without needing a small army of engineers. That said, the timing of a massive fundraise announcement alongside a product launch feels like the oldest playbook in Silicon Valley, so let's see if the model actually delivers before we get excited about what it means for your stack.

ai-at-work.title: AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter
ai-at-work.excerpt: There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measu
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AWS exec Colleen Aubrey is telling organizations to stop obsessing over AI-specific metrics and focus on actual business outcomes instead. This matters because too many digital workplace leaders are getting lost in the weeds measuring model accuracy or token usage when they should be asking if AI is actually making work faster, cheaper, or better. After thirty years in this space, I can tell you this is refreshing common sense in a field drowning in meaningless dashboards.

ai-at-work.title: Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but will Big Tech end up winning anyway?

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Politicians are getting interested in regulating AI and data centers, but early signals suggest Big Tech companies are navigating the heat just fine while infrastructure players are sweating. This matters because the regulatory environment directly shapes what tools and platforms your organization can actually deploy and how much you'll pay for them. Honestly, after thirty years watching Washington tinker with tech, I'd bet on Big Tech's lobbying budget over any politician's election promises any day of the week.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI buys tiny software developer to improve Codex
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI is buying Pierre Computer Company in order to incorporate the San Francisco-based software developer’s Code.Storage infrastructure layer for Git into its Codex AI-powered programming tool. Pier
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI just scooped up Pierre Computer Company, a tiny San Francisco shop with barely a dozen employees, to bolt their Code.Storage Git infrastructure into Codex, OpenAI's AI coding tool. This matters because it signals that enterprise AI tooling is getting serious about the plumbing layer, not just the flashy interface, which means your organization's version control and developer workflows are about to get a lot more interesting. The real takeaway is that even microscopic companies can catch the acquisition wave if they nail one thing really well, which should tell every workplace tech leader that sometimes the best solutions don't come from the usual suspects.

tools-tech.title: Box launches Architect, an AI-powered workflow builder
tools-tech.excerpt: Box has introduced a new natural-language AI tool that helps users build automated workflows around document-related processes. Box Architect, announced at BoxWorks 2026 on Thursday, “effectively acts
tools-tech.dwp_take: Box rolled out Architect, an AI tool that lets users build document automation workflows using natural language instead of traditional coding or configuration. This matters because it democratizes workflow automation for non-technical users, potentially reducing the bottleneck of having to wait for IT or developers to build these systems. My take: if it actually works as advertised, this is solid. If users still end up fiddling with the output for hours because the AI misunderstood their business logic, we're just trading one frustration for another.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft extends undisclosed usage restrictions on Copilot Chat for enterprise users
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft is extending undisclosed usage caps to additional Copilot Chat features for enterprise users who already pay for Microsoft 365 subscriptions but do not hold separate Microsoft 365 Copilot li
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is quietly capping how much free Copilot Chat access enterprise users get unless they buy a separate license, even though these folks already pay for Microsoft 365. This matters because it signals Microsoft is moving AI features from "included" to "upsell," which means your company's per-seat costs are about to creep up and your users will hit walls they didn't expect. After three decades watching this playbook, I'll say it plainly: this is classic vendor behavior, and your CFO should start budgeting for Copilot licenses now before someone upstream discovers the restrictions the hard way.

tools-tech.title: Don’t mention the data center: OpenAI calls them ‘compute campuses’ instead
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI has responded to the data center culture war pitting communities against tech companies with a proposal to reduce its power demand during periods of grid strain. The company is also mindful of
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI is rebranding data centers as "compute campuses" while promising to dial back power consumption during grid strain. For digital workplace pros, this matters because infrastructure naming directly affects how organizations communicate about hybrid work, AI tools, and the physical backbone that keeps remote teams functioning. Calling a data center a "compute campus" won't fool anyone who remembers when "cloud" was supposed to mean we'd never worry about physical infrastructure again, but hey, at least they're actually reducing power demand instead of just the terminology.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Democrats are planning to make workplace and labor issues central to their congressional agenda, even though legislative wins are unlikely given Republican control and Trump's veto power. This matters to digital workplace professionals because these debates shape compliance requirements, benefits policies, and how companies structure remote work arrangements and employee protections. Here's the thing: whether or not any of this becomes law, your HR and legal teams are already preparing for the conversation, which means more policy documents, more training modules, and more "please read and acknowledge" emails in your inbox.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece on five common mistakes people make during open enrollment season for health insurance. This matters to digital workplace pros because enrollment communication is often buried in terrible portals and confusing emails that actually drive the mistakes the article warns about. Here's the truth: if your benefits communication requires a decoder ring to understand, you've already lost half your workforce, which means higher support costs and angry employees come January.

digital-culture.title: ‘Bah, humbug!’ Could employee apathy mean curtains for the traditional holiday party?
digital-culture.excerpt: People say they prefer cash or time off, though some argue office gatherings are still beneficial
digital-culture.dwp_take: More employees are skipping or expressing indifference toward traditional holiday parties, with surveys showing they'd rather have cash bonuses or extra PTO instead. This matters because holiday gatherings have long been a cornerstone of workplace culture and informal connection, so shifting employee sentiment forces companies to rethink how they build community and show appreciation. Honestly, if your holiday party needs a mandatory attendance policy to survive, it probably wasn't doing much for morale anyway, and that's fine because most of them taste like sadness and spreadsheets anyway.

digital-culture.title: Ads in Chatbots Have Arrived. Here’s What’s Working—and What’s Not
digital-culture.excerpt: As Anthropic maintains its vow to keep ads out of Claude, the rest of the AI chatbot industry is racing to win over advertisers without antagonizing users.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic is holding firm against ads in Claude while competitors scramble to monetize their chatbots without driving users away. This matters because your enterprise AI tools will inevitably face the same pressure, and you need to know which platforms will stay clean versus which will turn into advertising cesspools. Here's my take: good luck, chatbot companies, because users will absolutely hate ads interrupting their work conversations, and I give most of these ad-supported models about eighteen months before they crater in user satisfaction.

industry-news.dwp_take: Nvidia is putting stricter tracking systems on GPU sales to Southeast Asian cloud providers because chips meant for that region keep ending up in China anyway. This matters to workplace tech folks because it signals that AI infrastructure supply chains are about to get messier, which means longer wait times and higher costs for companies trying to build out their AI capabilities. If you're planning an AI rollout, buckle up: the geopolitical chokehold on chips just got tighter.

industry-news.excerpt: Nothing CEO Carl Pei has confirmed a December launch for the company's first AI-native device. Here's what we know about its design, features, and availability. The post Nothing’s First AI Device Is C
industry-news.dwp_take: Nothing, Carl Pei's hardware company, is launching its first AI-native device this December with a focus on design and new features. Digital workplace pros need to watch this because AI devices are becoming workplace staples, and understanding how newcomers approach the category matters for your tech stack decisions. That said, "AI-native" has become the corporate equivalent of "blockchain" circa 2017, so I'll believe the innovation when I see it actually solve a real problem instead of just adding AI for the sake of it.

industry-news.title: Anthropic’s AI Progress Nearly Doubles: What IT Buyers Should Know
industry-news.excerpt: METR finds faster Anthropic AI benchmark progress, but key evidence remains redacted. Learn what IT buyers should check before adopting new model releases. The post Anthropic’s AI Progress Nearly Doub
industry-news.dwp_take: Anthropic claims their AI is progressing twice as fast according to benchmarks, though the actual data backing this up is still hidden from public view. If you're evaluating AI tools for your workplace, this matters because adopting the latest model without seeing the full evidence is like buying a car based on fuel economy claims you can't verify. I'd say wait for the redacted details before you start ripping out your current systems, because "trust me, it's better" has never been a solid procurement strategy in my three decades doing this work.

industry-news.title: This Week in Tech: AI Expands Everywhere as Security Threats and Infrastructure Pressures Mount
industry-news.excerpt: See what you missed in Daily Tech Insider from Nov. 2–6. The post This Week in Tech: AI Expands Everywhere as Security Threats and Infrastructure Pressures Mount appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: Organizations are rolling out AI tools across every corner of their operations while simultaneously dealing with escalating security vulnerabilities and aging infrastructure struggling under the load. This matters because digital workplace leaders are caught between the pressure to adopt AI and the reality that their systems weren't built to handle it safely, creating a genuine operational tension that no amount of vendor promises will solve. My take: we're basically watching companies try to install a Tesla engine into a 1987 Honda Civic and hope nobody notices the smoke.
